Content covers: the four mnemonic-pairs contrasting a lesser-seeming hardship against its seemingly milder counterpart (thoughts of transgression versus the act itself, an oven twice-heated versus a cold oven needing much wood, relearning forgotten material versus learning fresh, and old wall-clay versus fresh earth) each explained through Rashi's own everyday analogies; Rabbi Avahu's teaching on Rabbi's own etymology of 'dawn' via the hind's branching antlers (with the caveat that 'hind' is imprecise since females lack antlers); the extended discussion of why Esther is likened to both a hind and to dawn, including the Megillah 15b citation on Esther's own psalm-recitation at the house of idols and the divine abandonment she felt, and the Megillah 7a dispute over Esther's own canonical status; the resolution establishing the verse per Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet's own reading of 'dawn' as an expression of prayer (with the Isaiah 26 citation) rather than Rabbi's own reading via the hind, since a growing hind's antlers branch further each year just as accumulated prayer is heard; the mishnah's own dating question for the moonlit-mistake precedent, working through why it cannot be any ordinary day (requiring the High Priest specifically) and resolving it to Yom Kippur itself, with Rashi's own extended clarification that 'they brought the High Priest down' is a separate clause from the earlier 'they took it out to the place of burning,' returning to the Yom Kippur service's own order; and the baraita extending the night-slaughtered-invalid-offering's burning requirement to the bird-pinching and meal-offering-handful rites as well, since both stand in place of slaughtering, closing into 'what was, was, it cannot be undone,' continuing into a new teaching on 29b.
